Every order in Orders counts, including those with 0 invoices. The share is the order's count divided by the sum of per-order counts. The average share is taken over all orders. The output is the same three values.
"Their total number of invoices" is the sum of invoice counts across the above-average orders.
"Their total number of invoices" is the number of above-average orders, not the sum of their invoices.
"Their total number of invoices" is the total number of invoices in the whole database, not only for the above-average orders.

Shares are fractions between 0 and 1.
Shares are percentages (multiplied by 100).
"Strictly above" means share > average share, so orders equal to the average are excluded.

Some interpretations are missing:

The average amount by which the share exceeds the average share is the sum of the excesses divided by the number of all orders, not just the above-average ones.
Invoices are counted per order through Invoice_Line_Items (distinct invoice numbers) instead of from the Invoices table.

queries:
WITH oc AS (
  SELECT o.order_id, COUNT(i.invoice_number) AS cnt
  FROM Orders o
  LEFT JOIN Invoices i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
  GROUP BY o.order_id
),
s AS (
  SELECT order_id, cnt, CAST(cnt AS REAL) / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Invoices) AS share
  FROM oc
),
a AS (
  SELECT AVG(share) AS avg_share FROM s
)
SELECT SUM(cnt) AS total_invoice_count,
       AVG(share) AS mean_share,
       AVG(share - (SELECT avg_share FROM a)) AS mean_diff
FROM s
WHERE share > (SELECT avg_share FROM a);
SELECT order_id,
       CAST(COUNT(*) AS REAL) / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Invoices) AS share,
       AVG(CAST(COUNT(*) AS REAL) / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Invoices)) OVER () AS average_share
FROM Invoices
GROUP BY order_id;
WITH c AS (
  SELECT o.order_id, COUNT(i.invoice_number) AS cnt
  FROM Orders o
  LEFT JOIN Invoices i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
  GROUP BY o.order_id
),
s AS (
  SELECT cnt * 1.0 / (SELECT SUM(cnt) FROM c) AS share
  FROM c
)
SELECT MIN(share), MAX(share), AVG(share)
FROM s;
SELECT SUM(cnt) AS total_invoices
FROM (
  SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt
  FROM Invoices
  GROUP BY order_id
) t
WHERE cnt > (
  SELECT AVG(c)
  FROM (
    SELECT COUNT(*) AS c
    FROM Invoices
    GROUP BY order_id
  )
);
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS total_invoices
FROM Orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > (SELECT AVG(c) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS c FROM Orders GROUP BY customer_id));
SELECT order_id, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Invoices) AS total_invoices
FROM Order_Items
GROUP BY order_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > (SELECT AVG(c) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS c FROM Order_Items GROUP BY order_id));
